items.text: I agree with Misti Y that some people can love Cirque shows and still not like Le Reve, but that is really its own discussion. For me, the theater and visual design are the strong bits. The scenery and decor are absolutely breathtaking start to finish and the whole concept is beautiful and appealing. The problem is it doesn't quite work live. The storyline isn't especially fun and when I went to see it, the stage kept malfunctioning all evening, and it was hard to stay with it even during the better scenes. It's reaching for that Cirque spectacle but never quite gets there. I would recommend it mainly for the theater. Otherwise you might do better with another show.

I paid 38 dollars for a used mechanical keyboard and I think I got about 38 dollars worth maybe a little more. The space bar rattles and when I hit it with my thumbs it does this hollow clatter like you nudge a tray of cutlery. During the day I tune it out. After midnight I find myself typing around it. The E key repeats now and then so meeting becomes meeeting, happens maybe once every few paragraphs. Its rare enough to forget but frequent enough I reread everything before hitting send. I messaged the seller to ask what switches it was, got tired of waiting and bought it anyway. Answer came a week later after it was already on my desk. Brown switches for the record. Comfort is why I'm keeping it. Each key has a small bump partway down so my fingers know a press registered without slamming to bottom. I can get through a long email and my wrists feel fine afterward which my laptop keys never managed. I thought about sending it back. Return shipping would have eaten a real chunk of what I paid and I would have been back on the laptop. So it stays, rattle and all.

So I saw this show in Vegas recently. Its a circus style thing. I recommend it but its one star off for me. The storyline is kinda hard to follow and a few songs feel sleepy or just not right for the action. Still the performers are crazy, good athletic ability and physiques and aerobic skills. The women especially stand out, they go underwater for several minutes at a time. The theater is circular and the stage is circular too, so you get a good view from anywhere. There's three main entrances they use, and they become pretty important for major transitions. The stage and setting and lights are really pretty, memorable atmosphere. Tickets are pretty reasonable compared to big Vegas stuff like O and Love. I wanted more big effects like fire but that's not a huge deal. But you do have issues with the story and music. Even with that its an entertaining visually striking show and I recommend it.

I don't know if remote work is some magic fix for the whole industry. From my experience, from two years of mentoring five junior engineers, I feel it's overblown for the juniors. They don't need tickets and documentation and meetings. They need to sit in on design conversations and see how other people are debugging their issues and they need to be able to ask questions before they have spent hours confused. And that kind of interaction just happens organically in the office. If you're remote they need to know the right time to cut in, to set up a call and to explain a problem that they may not even fully understand. So it's a skill, and a tough one, to have before you have the chance to learn it. I've seen the feedback issues with remote work, short comments on a code review, it feels like it's the final word, not a learning opportunity. And it takes longer so less momentum. The juniors I mentored, they improved faster if they had in person pairing and whiteboard sessions and easy access to the seniors. I'm not trying to push for offices or anti flexibility. Remote work can be great for self driven devs. But for juniors, proximity is a booster, it gives confidence, context, and instincts. Sending jrs off with a laptop and a calendar can be a drag on junior development which can result in less good technical leadership in the future.

Elias was in the bakery, 3:17 AM. The mixer was running, that low hum in the soles of his boots. Flour dust in the air under the fluorescent light, looked like snowflakes stuck in the air. The sourdough loaves were on boards, crusts still pale and soft, before final bake. He wiped his hands on his apron, it was stiff with dough and sweat. He checked the lock at the front counter. Not that it was needed, more paranoia. He turned the key and went to the display case. The History of Salt, blue spine hardback with a crack near the hinge, was there. Every Thursday for 6 weeks, always on the glass case next to the unsold cinnamon rolls. No library stamp. The bakery is not part of the city system. He picked it up, cover cold. Opened it, thought it would be blank or have a forgotten bookmark. There was a folded square of lined paper that fell out on the counter. Unfolded it. Jagged handwriting, pressed hard. It said "You knead with your left hand dominant. Stop favoring the right. It ruins the tension." He looked at his hands, red knuckled, dusted white. The mixer went into next cycle. He closed the book, put it back on the glass, spine aligned with the edge. Turned off the light above the display, book in shadow.

My own experience would be to mention Apple. My school only allowed Apple computers for middle and high school kids. They were about twice as much as a PC. The computers broke about once a month. My own laptop i never dropped it once but i had to replace hard drive 5 times in 4 years and reinstall the OS multiple times. One extreme case was that a friends Macbook Pro caught fire while he was watching a movie. The smoke alarm went off. Apple support would not diagnose our problems. They would just backup and wipe it and restore the files.
My critique goes on to iPhones. I had the first iPhone and it would malfunction often. Now days Apple seemingly releases a new iphone about every 2 months and it is just a slightly better camera. I will grant one qualified good point, i pads are the best tablets, right now, but android tablets will get there eventually.

I went to see Awakening at the Wynn Las Vegas and it was fine but not something I would plan a whole trip around. I have been to Las Vegas constantly since I was a kid so I have seen a ton of shows before I turned 21 and I know what a production can be. The good news is the circular stage is smart. From almost any seat you can see the show and that is rare in big theater productions. If you are staying at Wynn or Encore there is a deal where tickets that are normally $125 are $99 for hotel guests and that does help. Some of the acts are impressive and the performers are strong. Aerialists, acrobats, whatever. But a lot of what they do is stuff I have seen done just as well in Cirque du Soleil shows. The bigger problem is the story, which is unclear or weak or basically not really there. I left not really knowing what the production was going for. And there was just too much going on, too many visuals, too many moving pieces, too many attempts at a wow. Less would hit harder. Other than a few cool stunts the whole thing felt average. I wasn't blown away and no one I was with seemed overwhelmed either. A few friends did like it, so if you have not seen it, maybe check it out especially with that hotel deal. But I would not see it again or pay full price a second time. It is the typical Vegas show where more is better and it just got messy.

I bought a skateboard at Zumiez then went back to get the rest of the equipment. At first the visit seemed positive. A female employee, my friend, his younger brother and I chatted while she assembled the board. She called herself a manager and said she's assembled boards every day throughout her employment and said if she was having a bad day and annoyed she would mistreat customers or other people. Then the assembly took about 90 minutes, I thought it would take no more than 15. She stripped two bolts then put them back in a way that made it look like they could be sold to another customer. She got her brother and another employee, described as a manager, to finish it or help with it. She was like, what is this? No apology. Zumiez has lost our future business. My heart was crushed.

Bought this mechanical keyboard second hand for $38, which is a steal. Communication with the seller was really bad, I messaged them about the switch type before buying and they took a full week to reply with one word. At that point I had already taken the gamble and ordered it.

The board is really well loved, space bar rattles bad, it sounds like loose Lego brick. The E key repeats occasionally. I get typos like theee instead of the. But I love typing on it. The feedback is great and super comfortable for long work emails. I did consider shipping it back but it's just too much hassle to send back a heavy slab of plastic that only cost $38. So I kept it and grew fond of it. Its flaws are fine, if you don't mind a bit of DIY tuning and an occasional double letter. Its a budget win.

Turkish Airlines you should be careful. So I booked Harbin to Beijing and then Turkish Airlines to Istanbul. Harbin flight delayed and I missed my connection. At Turkish booth, nobody would take responsibility or help me rebook. I stayed at airport overnight. Next morning I asked for ticket, they said overbooked, it could take days to get to Istanbul, unless I pay for business. And I needed to be in Istanbul. So I had no choice. I'm really angry and dont believe it can happen.

So you have to bring one broken household item for repair. When you get there, you need to get a numbered ticket from the registration desk. Keep the number safe. It decides where you are in the queue. The volunteer experts do the repairs first come first served. You have to get your thing back before the volunteers leave at 4pm. If you forget it, they will not keep it overnight. You have to make sure you have time to wait for your turn. They can't guarantee they can fix everything. Thanks for following these simple steps.

its a float valve controls trough filling. A float on a stem goes down and up with water level. When water is low float goes down, opens valve and water comes in. When water rises float goes up and closes valve. At the set level it shuts off. Two common reasons it overflows: dirt or minerals stuck in the valve so it does not close all the way. Or the float is set too high and valve only shuts off after the trough has already overflowed.

Went to a restaurant with a 10pm show at the same hotel, so figured it'd be easy. We arrived at 720 on Sunday, our names in their uselessly long list, told to pay at 823. Did, but stood around until 840 before they casually told us we'd be seated at 915. Not a party of 2. They had no solutions. If the wait is going to be past paying like that, tell people upfront. My night was completely wasted. Absolute disaster. Zero stars if you could give zero.

I am sorry. I know it is hard time. All the problems we have been facing inside Enron plus the world around us, it doesn't feel like holiday at all. A lot of people were not happy about it. Some thought it was a good chance for all Enron people to come together and celebrate. Others said just not appropriate. I understand both sides. After what has happened in the last month we have decided to cancel the party. Spending company money on celebration at this time could be seen as imprudent and that is a risk we don't want to take. You have all worked so hard and you deserve recognition and a reason to celebrate. We will find other more appropriate ways to recognize your great contributions during holiday season.

Ken Lay

A siphon moves water from one container to another. It uses gravity and air pressure to get the water over a high point between them. Its how it works: you fill the tube up with water so it is full with no air in it. Then it will flow. So the water goes down the long leg which goes down to the other container. So gravity pulls it down and when it goes down that pulls it down and creates a vacuum at the top of the siphon. And the atmospheric pressure will force water up the other leg so its full. And you have to have the outlet lower than the source water surface because the driving force is the weight difference between the two water columns. If the outlet is higher or at the same level, it won't pull it down enough to go up the intake side. The difference in gravity only works when the descending column is heavier. Air gets in, it breaks the chain. The air bubbles break the chain of water molecules and if it's broken it equalises the pressure in the tube with the outside. So it's stopped, it won't flow until you refill the tube with water again.

I found the sourdough on its second rise again. It's always a Thursday, always on the flour bin, and always the same copy of The Count of Monte Cristo with the Richmond Public Library stamp on it. I don't know how they get past the squeaky screen door without me hearing them, but honestly around 3:00 AM my brain is mostly yeast and caffeine anyway. Tonight though there was a scrap of yellow legal paper poking out of the top like a bookmark. I wiped my hands on my apron leaving a ghostly white smudge on the dark cloth and pulled it out. The note said in frantic spiky handwriting, Page 142. Please. I think they're watching the drop box now. A cold draft swept through the kitchen smelling of wet asphalt and oncoming rain. I looked toward the darkened front windows but all I saw was my own tired reflection staring back. I didn't open the book. Instead I carefully tucked the note back between the pages, slid the novel into a brown pastry bag and folded the top down twice to seal it.

I bought this used mechanical keyboard for $38 and I think I got about $38 worth of keyboard, maybe a bit more. The space bar is bad. It rattles. Its not a soft click, its a hollow loose clatter every time my thumb hits it. I stopped noticing it during the day but at night it sounds louder than it should. The E key also repeats sometimes. So meeting becomes meeeting. Happens once every few paragraphs, enough that I still proofread. Communication with seller was slow. I asked what switches it used before buying and the reply came a whole week later, after the board had already arrived. Its brown switches. The good part: its actually comfortable. The keys are nice to type on, with some cushioning to them. I can write long emails and my wrists dont complain. More than I can say for the laptop keyboard before. I considered sending it back but the hassle of it did not seem worth it. So its still on my desk. Rattling, repeating, but still doing its job. 3 stars.

hi everyone. so I'm [Name], Tom's brother. we shared a bunk bed till he was 14. Tom always slept on the top bunk and it was annoying and so loud snoring and they were fighting about who gets it every night. we were kids but I saw a lot of him and I've known him for a very long time. Tom is the most reliable guy. I forgot my passport once and Tom drove 6 hours to get it to me. He's the kind of brother that's loyal and generous, the kind that will go a stupidly far distance to save you from your own dumbness. That's Tom. so Tom. I'm really happy you found someone that loves you like we do and unlike me they decided to room with you voluntarily.

Le Reve I rated 4 stars unbiasedly, but for my own personal preference 2.5 stars. I never really wanted to see Cirque du Soleil before this, its my first. I expected lots of backflips and extreme acrobatics. But there was less of that and a lot of interpretive dancing, much more than I expected. Very impressive, but not my style. It's not for everyone, but if you like that kind of theatrical spectacle you'll probably love it. I wouldn't pay more than $100, but I got free tickets. Very glad I didn't have to pay.

Old style school attendance registers help historians sort out the day to day things like seasonal work, illness, bad weather, poverty, family stuff, moving around, local emergencies. They show which kids were there or not there, how regular they were, and sometimes why they missed school. And from this you can see how education fit in with work and household routines and what the community expected. Across years you can see habits of schooling changing or public health. And you can look at differences between boys and girls, age, neighborhood, class. But the problem is they only say what the school chose to note. They don't really tell you what it was like for the kids, and sometimes teachers put down stuff that's misreported, or incomplete, or just their own ideas. So they really work best when you check them against other sources.

It's always 2:17 every Thursday morning. Mara finds the book on the back step at the bakery. It's always the same one, A Field Guide to North American Moths. The county library sticker is ghost pale on the spine. There's a little flour worked into the jacket, as if the book had been helping. She's returned it twice, and the librarians smile too politely. By the third week she just kept it beside the rye starter and said nothing. Tonight it's raining and ticked against the alley door. The ovens are breathing. Mara is shaping croissants, pressing butter into dough, when the latch gives its tiny, guilty click. No one is there. Just the book, dry as a bone on the wet concrete. She wipes her hands on her apron and opens it. Between Luna Moth and Promethea there's a slip of paper folded once. It says: Your window is the only light on this street. I read here until the first bus. I'm sorry about the crumbs. Mara looks at the alley, the dented milk crates and steam rising off the drains. For a second the city felt enormous, then it did not. She tears a corner from an order pad and writes: Cinnamon rolls come out at 4:05. Then she puts the note inside the book and places it on the warm windowsill, and unlocks the back door.

We tried out some folded cardboard bridges for our classroom project. We made beam, arch like, and triangular fold ones. It's the same cardboard and we tried to keep the length and width about the same. We put each between two supports, and we put little weights on them one by one and saw how they bend or tip or break. It's handmade and we only did a few tests, so it's not real engineering data. The triangular fold ones seemed to hold more weight better. So the way you fold them can affect how well they hold weight.

Marguerite found the book on the steel table by the back door, under the bench where the bread peels hang. Its title is A Field Guide to Coastal Birds. Inside the cover there is a stamp from the Harbor Street branch, due date is March. The mail slot in that door was nailed shut years ago but the delivery hatch next to it, the one the flour man used, never latched properly. She asked the day staff. She checked the hatch for scratches. Once she stayed past four with her coat on. Eleven Thursdays. Nothing. The book turned up between two and four, and she was at the ovens with her back to the door every time. Tonight there was a grocery receipt from Pell's folded into the page on oystercatchers. The ink was blotchy where someone pressed too hard. The note reads I keep meaning to take this back to the library, then I pass your door and there is the smell of bread and I put it down instead. I can stop if you want. She smelled of salt, she thought, whoever it was, because the pages did. Marguerite pulled a pencil from her apron and wrote on the back of the receipt. Bring it Thursday. I'll have a roll. She tucked it in at the oystercatchers, set the book on the hatch ledge, and put a warm roll in a paper bag beside it.

I moved to Toronto so I don't use Hydro Ottawa any more but I want to warn others about their billing stuff. I had an account for a year when I rented a downtown apartment. Then I moved back in with my parents to do an MA so I cancelled the account and paid off all the charges. But even after cancelling they kept taking money from a different bank account of mine at random times for over a year. I called their customer service over and over and sent them proof of the withdrawals. The reps would tell me my account was closed and no debits were happening. I had to check utility bills with my parents and see that they had linked my bank details to my parents' billing number just because I said I was moving home. My parents didn't notice because they kept getting refunds for overpayments so it looked normal. I spent hours on the phone talking to several reps before a manager looked into it. The manager confirmed the mistake and fixed it. But they wouldn't refund me at first and only offered an apology. I never will put my banking details in for auto debit again. Their reckless handling of data should worry all consumers.

It was 3:40 on the Thursday morning. I was there and the second batch of rye was proofing. I found it again. A book on the flour bin by the back door. It was cold from the alley. Same book, A Field Guide to Night Birds, Eastgate Branch library. Was due 3 weeks ago. And this is the 4th Thursday I found it. I have carried it to the drop box every week. Every Thursday it's back. As if the building is borrowing it. So I wiped my hands on my apron and opened it up. I found a folded index card. It was stuck to the barn owls page. It said you leave the vent fan on. The alley smells like bread until 5. I walk my mother's dog then because she can't anymore. I keep forgetting to return this. Maybe I keep not wanting to. Signed R. I read it twice while the oven timer counted down. Outside the fan was humming and pushed warm air into the dark. Then I turned the card over. I wrote on it with the grease pencil that I use for marking trays. I wrote that the rye is out at 4:15. And I tore a heel off of yesterday's loaf. Wrapped it in wax paper, put the book on top of it and propped the back door open by one inch.

I used Ryanair when I was a poor student, for going to Sweden, because my ex-partner lived there. It was the cheapest way to get there. The whole experience was awful. I was at the airport, and they took my L'Occitane shower gel, a £20 bottle, and they said it's over the liquid limit, but it wasn't. I could go to the airport pharmacy and buy a 100ml bottle and get it back. So I did that, went back, and they said they don't know what I was talking about. So £20 gone. I was really angry. Also at the gate they charged me another £5 because I had a bottle of water in my hand luggage, which I'd bought inside the airport. And now Ryanair stopped flying from Liverpool John Lennon Airport to Stockholm Skavsta, so I fly Norwegian Air now. Their customer service is bad too, ironically, but at least the planes feel newer and less old than Ryanair's.

So you're not the only one, I had a very wet day on Tuesday and by Thursday half my brandy wines had split. You can see the seam right down the side of the fruit. It's the same old story, dry spell then all the rain in one go. The inside of the fruit takes water in faster than the skin can stretch to keep up. The Sungolds are mostly ok for now but a few look like they'll follow. Once the weather has done it you really can't get around it. The only thing that helps a bit is keeping the 2 day schedule on a more even footing. It doesn't matter much once the sky decides to let it all out at once. You'll probably get a good crop from the rest of the vines. Just pick the split ones off and put them to some other use. Its a lot more of a headache with the brandy wines, that thick skin they have is a real liability in a storm like this. You might get better luck with the Sungolds if you can keep them from getting quite so much water in a single go.

The College Board is really hypocritical. A friend of mine took a one-hour SAT Subject Test and the proctor gave her room like twenty extra minutes by mistake. She knew it was an unfair advantage and she really values integrity so she reported it to their official hotline, to prevent future stuff.

But the result? Total institutional injustice. After an investigation, the College Board said there was not enough evidence to hold the proctor or other students accountable. But they did find enough evidence of misconduct by my friend and canceled her scores. So they punish the one who is honest, while letting the real violators go. How unfair and broken this organization is.

Thursdays the book shows up. Not on the counter, mind you, but wedged behind the flour bins by the back door. Whoever leaves it knows exactly where I won't trip over it. Its always the same book, A Field Guide to North American Moths, from the Elmwood Branch. The due date is stamped so long ago the ink has gone violet. I've never actually seen anyone drop it off. I'm elbow deep in rye dough by 2pm and honestly at that hour I wouldn't notice a marching band. For the first few weeks I just put it on the shelf by the register. By Friday morning it was gone. Thursday it was back. Fine, people are strange. I'm a guy who talks to his sourdough starter so I'm not judging. Tonight there's a note tucked at page 114, the luna moths. It reads: They only live a week. They don't even eat. I keep thinking that's a waste of a beautiful thing. Do you ever get to see the bread before its gone. No signature. Just pencil pressed hard. I read it twice, then a third time while the ovens ticked. Then I pulled the first loaf of the night, still crackling. Wrapped it in brown paper and set it behind the flour bins.

So if you walk in and the room feels stifling, it is just a temperature thing. It could be a comfortable temp, but still stuffy. Humidity plays a role. High humidity doesn't let moisture evaporate off your skin, so the air feels heavy, stale. Airflow matters too. If no movement of air then CO2, smells, heat, just stays around people. Bad venting. So the room feels close, oppressive. AC is just cooling air, not lowering humidity, not improving circulation. Open the window, fan, or venting, and you will get a better feel. It just moves air and lowers the moisture.

I've mentored five junior engineers for the last two years and i think i have a better perspective. It's not a win for everyone. Remote work is great for people who can direct their own efforts and know what they want to do. But it's a lot more difficult for people who are learning. You get told remote work is a win for everybody and it isn't. These people don't need tickets, docs, or scheduled meetings. What they need is to get in on design arguments, watch somebody else get through a nasty bug, and get answers before a little uncertainty snowballs. You get all of that for free in an office. Work from home and they have to figure out when to interrupt, get a call set up, and explain a problem they probably don't get yet. That is a steep thing to ask of someone who hasn't had the chance to learn it.

I've watched that setup screw up feedback. A short note on a code review ends up reading like a final judgment. The lag on getting answers kills forward motion. The people I worked with moved ahead a lot quicker when they could pair up in person, work through things on a whiteboard, and actually get hold of the seniors. None of this means you should scrap flexibility. But for a beginner, being around other people is what gets them there. It's how they pick up the confidence, context, and judgment they need. You are going to end up with weaker technical leadership down the road if you just hand a newcomer a laptop and a calendar.

A simple rain gauge just catches rain falling into an opening of known area. They usually report the result as depth in millimetres or inches. What this shows is how much water would cover flat ground if nothing drained, evaporated or soaked in. Many gauges use a funnel with a wide opening, that feeds a narrower measuring tube. The same amount of water will rise higher in a narrow tube, so it makes small amounts of rain easier to read. The scale on the tube is marked to account for the area ratio, so you still get a true rainfall depth. Wind is a common source of error. Gusts around the gauge can carry raindrops past the opening, so it undercounts. Evaporation or splashing before reading can also distort the results.

I bought this keyboard used for $38. As soon as I pulled it out of the box it felt fair, it did have some dust between the keys and a few shiny spots on the caps but nothing worse than I expected from a second-hand board. The good part, it is genuinely comfortable. I write long emails for work and my hands feel less cramped than they did on my flat office keyboard. The switches have a steady feel not too heavy and the case does not slide around on my desk. There are problems though. The space bar rattles every time I hit it, it is loud enough that I notice it during quiet mornings. One key the e, occasionally repeats so I get words like neeed if I type too fast. It doesn't happen constantly but it happens enough that I proofread more carefully. I also asked the seller what switches it had and they answered a full week later, after the keyboard had already arrived. Not great. Still, for $38 I kept it. Shipping it back felt like more trouble than the keyboard was worth.

So bring one broken thing per person, check in at the front table and get a numbered ticket, keep it until your stuff gets fixed. Volunteers call numbers in order. Stay around because sometimes they need you or your decision. Not everything can be repaired, parts need to be ordered, some stuff can't be fixed. Get your stuff before volunteers leave at 4:30pm or if it is not picked up, they can't store it.

I went to this buffet on a Friday around 4:30 p.m. Surprisingly there was no line at all. The bill came out to about 130 dollars for two people, which felt pretty steep. I figured before going that it would be comparable to a steak house. Afterward I learned it cost somewhat more than I had expected to pay at one. I was disappointed the steak wasn’t offered. At that price I assumed there would be some kind of steak option. The meats included lamb, prime rib and chicken, but those are things you can find at other Las Vegas buffets for much less money.

The seafood station had Alaskan crab legs and rock crab claws. Alaskan crab legs are available at a lot of Vegas buffets but I hadn’t run into rock crab claws anywhere else, so those were interesting. The problem was there were no crab crackers. Staff said wooden mallets were available, but our table was so close to the next table I didn’t want to start smashing shells and send pieces flying at the people next to us. So I just ate the legs. The Asian station didn’t seem especially distinctive either, it reminded me quite a bit of the buffet at Rampart Casino. Dessert had gelato and various pastries, nothing really stood out. They had fresh juices, although I didn’t try any.

I’d call this buffet acceptable but overpriced for what it offers. If you’re curious it’s worth trying once, especially if there’s no wait. But if the line is long I’d probably reconsider.

Old school attendance registers are really valuable to historians who want to see what daily life looked like. They track when students showed up. From these you can see patterns from farming seasons, local sickness, or bad weather. For example if attendance suddenly drops, it could be that flu hit the area or harvest time meant the kids had to work. This shows how education had to compete with money. Then you might see some groups not showing up much, which would point to social inequality or people not caring about school. But historians have to be careful. The records can be inconsistent or even made up. Teachers or headmasters might have fiddled with numbers so they got more funding or avoided being questioned. So the numbers dont always mean what actually happened. Also the registers usually just say the kid was there or not, not why. So we have to use other sources to guess why. All you get from the logs is numbers for understanding community life. But you need to compare with other evidence to really know what was going on.

I know Apple well, this is just experience. My school only allowed Apple computers for middle and high school students. They were twice as expensive and they broke every month. I never dropped my laptop but in four years I replaced the hard drive five times and reinstalled the operating system to keep it working. So the float valve on the cattle trough works like this. Its connected to a pressurized water line. The float is a plastic ball or block, it's buoyant and rests on the water surface. Its connected to a lever arm. When the animals drink the level drops, the float sinks, this tilts the arm, pulls the plunger or washer away from the valve seat and water flows in. As the water goes up the float lifts with it. The lever pushes the plunger back to the seat, it gradually narrows the opening until the flow stops at the set level. It overflows if the washer is worn or dirty and can't seal, or if the float got punctured and waterlogged and no longer rises enough to close the valve.
